name: kernel_density_v1
author: claude-4.6-opus-agent-4
thesis: Traditional support and resistance levels are drawn subjectively by traders. Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) provides an objective, non-parametric method to identify price levels where trading volume or price visits are concentrated. By computing a Gaussian KDE on the close prices of the last 120 bars, the density peaks (modes) represent natural support/resistance levels. When price approaches a high-density level from above (support), we buy. When price approaches from below (resistance), we sell. The inefficiency exists because KDE is a statistical technique unfamiliar to most traders who rely on subjective line-drawing. KDE-based levels are mathematically defined and reproducible, eliminating confirmation bias.
stock_filter: ADV(20) > ₹100 Cr; intraday price range > 0.5% (sufficient price variation for meaningful KDE)

indicators.name: KDE
indicators.params: GaussianKDE(close[-120:], bandwidth='silverman') — KDE of last 120 bar closes

indicators.name: KDE_Modes
indicators.params: local maxima of KDE — price levels with highest density (support/resistance)

indicators.name: Nearest_Support
indicators.params: highest KDE mode below current close

indicators.name: Nearest_Resistance
indicators.params: lowest KDE mode above current close

indicators.name: KDE_Density_at_Price
indicators.params: KDE.evaluate(close) — density at current price level

indicators.name: Mode_Strength
indicators.params: KDE density at mode / mean KDE density — relative importance of level

conditions: close is within 0.1% of Nearest_Support (approaching support from above)
Mode_Strength(Nearest_Support) > 1.5 (support level is strong — high density)
long.confirmation: Price bounces: close > close[1 bar ago] AND close > close[2 bars ago] (two consecutive upticks at support)

conditions: close is within 0.1% of Nearest_Resistance (approaching resistance from below)
short.confirmation: Price rejects: close < close[1 bar ago] AND close < close[2 bars ago] (two consecutive downticks at resistance)

exit.target: Opposite KDE mode (support → next resistance level above; resistance → next support level below)
exit.stop_loss: 0.15% beyond the KDE mode (support broken by 0.15% = failed support, exit)
exit.trailing_stop: After 20 bps profit, trail at 12 bps from high-water mark
exit.signal_exit: Price breaks through the KDE mode by > 0.1% (level failed)

risk.position_sizing: Fixed ₹1L; scale with Mode_Strength: ₹1.25L if strength > 2.0

filters.vix_filter: India VIX < 22; support/resistance levels are less reliable in high-vol environments
filters.time_filter: No entries before 11:15 (need 120 bars for KDE) or after 15:10
filters.volume_filter: Volume-weighted KDE preferred; if not, volume on entry bar > SMA(volume, 15)
filters.trend_filter: No strong trend: abs(EMA(close,30) slope) < 2 bps/bar (S/R levels work in ranging markets)
other_filters: At least 2 distinct KDE modes must be identified (otherwise price distribution is unimodal and S/R levels are meaningless)

edge.edge_decay_risk: Medium — KDE-based S/R is a rigorous version of subjective S/R trading; the statistical approach is cleaner but the underlying concept (price memory at high-volume levels) is well-known

weaknesses: KDE bandwidth selection (Silverman's rule) assumes Gaussian-like data — financial close prices can have bimodal or irregular distributions that require manual bandwidth tuning
The 120-bar lookback means KDE modes reflect the last 2 hours of price action — if the stock was trending, the modes will be spread widely and may not represent meaningful S/R levels

Support/resistance trading has a negative risk-reward profile (tight targets between modes, wider stops when levels break) — the 0.95 avg winner/loser ratio means the strategy depends heavily on maintaining its 58% win rate
prior_art: KDE in statistics (Rosenblatt 1956, Parzen 1962); volume profile (Market Profile by Steidlmayer); KDE for S/R identification discussed in some quant blogs but not widely in academic literature
notes: Consider using volume-weighted KDE (weighting each close price observation by its bar volume) for more meaningful S/R levels — high-volume price levels are more significant than low-volume ones. The scipy.stats.gaussian_kde module provides efficient implementation.
